Most U.S. sanctions run through a two-step framework: the National Emergencies Act sets how emergencies are declared and ended, and IEEPA supplies the economic powers once one is declared. Country-specific acts then write some programs into statute and limit the President's ability to lift them. This is the clearest example in the wiki of the layer structure: framework statutes below, specific authorizations on top.

## What you should be able to do

- Trace a sanctions program from emergency declaration to blocking order.
- Explain what changed when IEEPA replaced the peacetime use of TWEA.
- Identify statutes that limit a President's ability to lift sanctions.

## Reading path

Read these in order. Each card links to the wiki page and to the official text. Ticking a box saves your progress in this browser only.

::: {.reading-card .domain-war-powers data-statute="nea-1976"}
[National Emergencies Act](../../statutes/nea-1976.qmd) [1976]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Framework statute]{.layer-badge}

Ended the open-ended emergencies that had accumulated since the 1930s and set procedures for declaring, renewing, and terminating national emergencies.

[Read it: [enacted text](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/statute/90/1255), [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/50/1601?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="nea-1976"> I have read this</label>
:::

::: {.reading-card .domain-aid-sanctions data-statute="ieepa-1977"}
[IEEPA](../../statutes/ieepa-1977.qmd) [1977]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Framework statute]{.layer-badge}

The workhorse of U.S. economic sanctions. After declaring a national emergency over an unusual and extraordinary threat that originates largely abroad, the President may block property and prohibit transactions involving foreign countries, entities, and individuals.

[Read it: [enacted text](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/statute/91/1625), [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/50/1701?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="ieepa-1977"> I have read this</label>
:::

::: {.reading-card .domain-aid-sanctions data-statute="twea-1917"}
[Trading with the Enemy Act](../../statutes/twea-1917.qmd) [1917]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Framework statute]{.layer-badge}

A First World War statute giving the President sweeping control over trade and property involving enemy countries and nationals.

[Read it: [enacted text](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/statute/40/411), [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/50/4305?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="twea-1917"> I have read this</label>
:::

::: {.reading-card .domain-aid-sanctions data-statute="caatsa-2017"}
[CAATSA](../../statutes/caatsa-2017.qmd) [2017]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Specific authorization]{.layer-badge}

A three-part sanctions law aimed at Iran, Russia, and North Korea. Its Russia title wrote existing executive order sanctions into statute and gave Congress the power to block the President from easing them.

[Read it: [enacted text](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/115/public/44), [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/22/9401?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="caatsa-2017"> I have read this</label>
:::

::: {.reading-card .domain-aid-sanctions data-statute="glomag-2016"}
[Global Magnitsky Act](../../statutes/glomag-2016.qmd) [2016]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Specific authorization]{.layer-badge}

Authorizes visa bans and asset freezes against foreign individuals and entities responsible for serious human rights abuse or significant corruption anywhere in the world.

[Read it: [enacted text](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/114/public/328), [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/22/10101?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="glomag-2016"> I have read this</label>
:::

::: {.reading-card .domain-aid-sanctions data-statute="iran-sanctions-1996"}
[Iran Sanctions Act](../../statutes/iran-sanctions-1996.qmd) [1996]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Specific authorization]{.layer-badge}

Originally the Iran and Libya Sanctions Act. It pioneered secondary sanctions by penalizing foreign companies, not just U.S. ones, that invest in Iran's energy sector.

[Read it: [enacted text](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/104/public/172), [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/50/1701?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="iran-sanctions-1996"> I have read this</label>
:::

::: {.reading-card .domain-aid-sanctions data-statute="inara-2015"}
[Iran Nuclear Review Act](../../statutes/inara-2015.qmd) [2015]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Specific authorization]{.layer-badge}

Gives Congress a defined period to review any nuclear agreement with Iran before the President may waive or suspend statutory sanctions, and requires regular compliance certifications afterward.

[Read it: [enacted text](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/114/public/17), [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/42/2160e?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="inara-2015"> I have read this</label>
:::

## Further reading

- [Helms-Burton Act](../../statutes/helms-burton-1996.qmd){.subj}: Wrote the Cuba embargo into statute so that a President cannot lift it alone, and extended its reach to foreign companies that use property confiscated by the Cuban government.
- [Caesar Act](../../statutes/caesar-2019.qmd){.subj}: Imposed secondary sanctions on foreign persons doing business with the Assad government's military, energy, aviation, and reconstruction sectors.
- [Section 232 (trade)](../../statutes/sec232-1962.qmd){.subj}: Allows the President to restrict imports that threaten to impair national security. The Commerce Department investigates and reports, and the President then decides whether to impose tariffs, quotas, or negotiated limits.
- [AEDPA (terrorism)](../../statutes/aedpa-1996.qmd){.subj}: Passed after the Oklahoma City bombing. Its national security significance lies in two linked provisions: the Secretary of State's power to designate foreign terrorist organizations, and the crime of giving such organizations material support.
- [Section 2808 (construction)](../../statutes/sec2808-milcon-1982.qmd){.subj}: One of the standby powers unlocked by a national emergency. When a declared war or emergency requires use of the armed forces, the Secretary of Defense may build military construction projects that Congress never authorized, using unspent military construction funds.

## Key terms

**National emergency**
:   A presidential declaration under the National Emergencies Act that unlocks standby statutory powers. The President must specify which powers are being used, and emergencies lapse unless renewed each year.

**Blocking**
:   Freezing property and interests in property within U.S. jurisdiction and prohibiting transactions in them, the core tool of IEEPA sanctions.

**Secondary sanctions**
:   Penalties on foreign persons, not just U.S. persons, for dealing with a sanctioned country or sector. The Iran Sanctions Act pioneered them.

## Check yourself

Try to answer each question before opening it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 1. What must a President do before using IEEPA's powers?

Declare a national emergency under the [National Emergencies Act](../../statutes/nea-1976.qmd) over an unusual and extraordinary threat that originates largely outside the United States. See [IEEPA](../../statutes/ieepa-1977.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 2. Why did Congress pass IEEPA in 1977?

Between 1933 and 1977 Section 5(b) of the [Trading with the Enemy Act](../../statutes/twea-1917.qmd) was used in peacetime emergencies as an all-purpose sanctions power. IEEPA moved peacetime use into a separate statute tied to the new emergency procedures.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 3. How did CAATSA change the President's control of Russia sanctions?

Its Russia title wrote existing executive order sanctions into statute and gave Congress a procedure to block the President from easing them. See [CAATSA](../../statutes/caatsa-2017.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 4. What does the Global Magnitsky Act let the executive do, and to whom?

Impose visa bans and asset freezes on foreign individuals and entities responsible for serious human rights abuse or significant corruption anywhere in the world. See [Global Magnitsky Act](../../statutes/glomag-2016.qmd).
:::
